title: Manganese Deficiency in Plants: Signs, Causes and How to Fix It
metaTitle: Manganese Deficiency in Plants: Signs and Fixes
metaDescription: Manganese deficiency shows on the young leaves first. See the signs crop by crop, what causes it, and the fertilizer sold here that fixes it.
excerpt: Manganese deficiency in plants starts on the young leaves and the growing tip. Manganese switches on many enzymes and works in the part of photosynthesis that splits water and releases oxygen. It also helps the plant make chlorophyll and protein. Here are the signs in each crop, what brings it, how to be sure and the fertilizer that fixes it.

blocks.text: Manganese is very immobile in the plant, so the first signs show on the young leaves. The old leaves stay green until the shortage gets severe.
Manganese deficiency symptoms

Young leaves turn pale yellow between the veins, often as a fine mottle of tiny yellow spots, while the veins stay green. Rice and corn show grayish green specks or streaks on the young leaves, which later turn yellow, orange and brown. New leaves come out short and narrow, and plants stay small with smaller roots. In rice, plants short of manganese also get more brown spot disease.
Manganese deficiency by crop

Each crop shows it its own way. So find yours in the tables below, then open its page for the photo and the full fix, like the one for [manganese in rice](/nutrient-deficiencies/rice-nutrient-deficiency#manganese).

blocks.text: What causes manganese deficiency

Manganese shortage comes on calcareous, alkaline and over limed soils, because high pH locks it up. Neutral soils high in organic matter, leached sandy soils, and old, highly weathered or degraded soils low in manganese also run short. Upland rice and other dryland crops suffer more than flooded rice, because flooding makes manganese more soluble.
How to be sure it is manganese

Iron shortage also yellows young leaves, but it is a smooth yellow that can turn white, while manganese gives a speckled mottle. Magnesium shortage looks alike between the veins but starts on the old leaves, and manganese shortage often comes with phosphorus shortage. A soil test for manganese at a DA Regional Soils Laboratory, read together with the soil pH, shows the risk. A leaf tissue test is the more accurate check, because it measures what the plant actually takes up.
How to fix manganese deficiency

On high pH soils the soil ties up manganese fast. So band manganese sulfate near the row or spray it instead of broadcasting. Use ammonium sulfate instead of urea to acidify the root zone. Add manure or straw where soil manganese and organic matter are low. Let the soil and tissue tests decide the rate.
Manganese sulfate works well as a spray. A typical rate in a Haifa vegetable guide is about 100 grams per 100 liters of water. Two or three sprays are sometimes needed for a full response.

How to keep manganese deficiency away
Do not over lime, and on soils known to be low in manganese keep the pH near neutral rather than high. Use acidifying fertilizers such as ammonium sulfate and keep returning organic matter.

blocks.title: Too much is a problem too
blocks.text: On strongly acid soils below about pH 5.5, manganese turns toxic, giving crumpled leaves with dark brown specks and dead leaf edges. Toxic manganese levels have also been found in Central Luzon rice soils, and liming acid soils is the usual cure.

blocks.text: Manganese deficiency questions

items.q: What does manganese deficiency look like?
items.a: Young leaves turn pale between green veins, often as a fine speckled mottle, and later show brown spots. In rice and corn the young leaves show grayish green specks or streaks.

items.q: What is the best fertilizer for manganese deficiency?
items.a: Manganese sulfate is the most common source, used as a spray or banded near the row. Broadcasting it on high pH soil works poorly because the soil ties it up.

items.q: Why does my soil have manganese but my plants are short of it?
items.a: High pH and lots of organic matter lock manganese into forms roots cannot take, even when the soil holds plenty. A leaf tissue test shows what the plant really gets.

items.q: Can too much manganese harm my crop?
items.a: Yes. On very acid soils below about pH 5.5, manganese can turn toxic and crumple the leaves with dark specks. Liming the soil by the soil test fixes it.
